lesson.title: Setting Up VS Code
lesson.description: Learn what an IDE is, install Python and Visual Studio Code, and create and run your first .py file.

blocks.title: Your coding workshop
blocks.text:
You *could* write code in a plain text app like Notepad, but programmers use tools made for the job.

An **IDE** (**Integrated Development Environment**) puts everything you need to write code in one place, like a workshop with all the tools on the wall:
- An **editor** that colours your code so it's easier to read
- **Autocomplete** that suggests code as you type
- A way to **run** your program with one click
- A **debugger** to help you find and fix bugs
- A built-in **terminal** to type commands

## Code editor or IDE?
A **code editor** is lighter and simpler. An **IDE** has every tool built in. **Visual Studio Code** sits in the middle: it's a code editor that becomes IDE-like once you add **extensions**.

blocks.title: Key words
blocks.text: Tap each card to reveal what it means.

items.title: IDE
items.text: Integrated Development Environment: one app with all the tools for writing, running and fixing code.

items.title: Code editor
items.text: A lighter app for writing code, with colours and helpful shortcuts.

items.title: Extension
items.text: An add-on that gives VS Code new features, such as Python support.

items.title: Terminal
items.text: A window where you type commands to the computer, like running a Python file.

items.title: Debugger
items.text: A tool that runs your code step by step so you can find bugs.

items.title: Syntax highlighting
items.text: Colouring different parts of code so it's easier to read.

blocks.title: What does IDE stand for?
blocks.explanation: IDE stands for Integrated Development Environment.

blocks.title: Meet Visual Studio Code
blocks.text:
**Visual Studio Code** (often shortened to **VS Code**) is a free code editor made by **Microsoft** and first released in 2015. It runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, and it's one of the most popular tools programmers use.

> Don't mix it up with **Visual Studio**, a different and much bigger Microsoft IDE. You want **Visual Studio Code**, the one with the blue icon.

items.title: Works with many languages
items.text: Python, JavaScript, HTML, C++ and many more, all in one app.

items.title: IntelliSense
items.text: Smart autocomplete that suggests code and shows information as you type.

items.title: Extensions
items.text: Thousands of free add-ons, such as Python support, themes and helpers.

items.title: Built-in terminal
items.text: Run commands and programs without leaving the editor.

items.title: Debugging
items.text: Pause your program and step through it line by line to find bugs.

items.title: Git support
items.text: Save versions of your work and share it, built right in.

items.title: Python isn't included
items.text: VS Code doesn't come with Python. You install Python separately, plus the Python extension.

items.title: Needs some setup
items.text: Out of the box it's a plain editor. Most features come from extensions you choose.

items.title: Can slow down
items.text: Installing lots of extensions can make it start and run more slowly.

items.title: Lots of settings
items.text: There are hundreds of options, which can feel overwhelming at first. The defaults are fine to start with.

items.title: Not a specialist tool
items.text: Tools like PyCharm are built just for Python and have more advanced features for very large projects.

blocks.title: Which statements about VS Code are true? Select all that apply.
blocks.explanation: VS Code is free, made by Microsoft and extended with add-ons, but Python must be installed separately.

options.text: It comes with Python already installed
You can add features with extensions

blocks.title: Python comes first
blocks.text:
VS Code is where you **write** code, but you need **Python** itself to **run** it. Install Python first.

Go to **python.org/downloads** and download the latest version of **Python 3**. Then follow the steps for your computer below.

> Ask a parent, guardian or teacher before installing software if this isn't your own computer.

items.title: Installing Python on Windows
items.text:
1. On python.org, click **Download Python 3.x**.
2. Open the downloaded installer.
3. **Important:** at the bottom of the first screen, tick **Add python.exe to PATH**.
4. Click **Install Now** and wait for it to finish.
5. To check it worked, open **Command Prompt** and type:
```bash
python --version
```
You should see something like `Python 3.13.0`.

items.title: Installing Python on macOS
items.text:
1. On python.org, click **Download Python 3.x** to get the macOS installer (a `.pkg` file).
2. Open it and follow the steps, clicking **Continue** and then **Install**.
3. To check it worked, open **Terminal** and type:
```bash
python3 --version
```
On a Mac, use `python3` instead of `python`.

items.title: Installing Python on Linux
items.text:
Most Linux systems already have Python 3. Open a terminal and check:
```bash
python3 --version
```
If it's missing on Ubuntu or Debian, install it with:
```bash
sudo apt install python3
```

blocks.title: When installing Python on Windows, which box should you tick?
blocks.explanation: Ticking Add python.exe to PATH lets your computer find Python when you type `python`.

blocks.title: Download VS Code
blocks.text: Go to **code.visualstudio.com**. The site usually detects your computer and shows the right download button. Then follow the steps for your system.

blocks.title: Install VS Code on your computer

items.title: Installing VS Code on Windows
items.text:
1. Click **Download for Windows** and open the installer.
2. Accept the agreement and click **Next**.
3. On **Select Additional Tasks**, keep **Add to PATH** ticked. Ticking **Add "Open with Code" action** is handy too.
4. Click **Install**, then **Finish** to launch VS Code.

items.title: Installing VS Code on macOS
items.text:
1. Click **Download for macOS**. You'll get a `.zip` file.
2. Open it to unzip **Visual Studio Code.app**.
3. Drag **Visual Studio Code.app** into your **Applications** folder.
4. Open it from Applications or Launchpad. If macOS asks whether you're sure, click **Open**.

items.title: Installing VS Code on Linux
items.text:
1. Download the **.deb** file (Ubuntu/Debian) or **.rpm** file (Fedora).
2. On Ubuntu/Debian, install it from the terminal in your Downloads folder:
```bash
sudo apt install ./code_*.deb
```
3. Or install it as a Snap:
```bash
sudo snap install code --classic
```

blocks.title: Add the Python extension
blocks.text:
Next, give VS Code Python superpowers:
1. Open VS Code.
2. Click the **Extensions** icon on the left (four squares), or press `Ctrl+Shift+X` (`Cmd+Shift+X` on a Mac).
3. Search for **Python**.
4. Choose the one published by **Microsoft** and click **Install**.

This adds the **Run** button, autocomplete and error hints for Python.

blocks.title: Which Python extension should you install?
blocks.explanation: The official Python extension is published by Microsoft.

options.text: Any extension with a snake icon
None: Python support is built in
The one with the fewest downloads

items.title: 1. Make a folder for your code
items.text:
Keep all your code in one place. Create a folder such as **Python Projects** in your **Documents** folder.
- **Windows:** in File Explorer, right-click → **New** → **Folder**
- **macOS:** in Finder, **File** → **New Folder**

items.title: 2. Open the folder in VS Code
items.text: In VS Code, click **File** → **Open Folder…** (on a Mac, **File** → **Open…**), choose your **Python Projects** folder and click **Select Folder** (or **Open**).

items.title: 3. Trust the folder
items.text: VS Code may ask: *Do you trust the authors of the files in this folder?* It's your own folder, so click **Yes, I trust the authors**.

items.title: 4. Create a new file
items.text:
In the **Explorer** panel on the left (`Ctrl+Shift+E`), hover over your folder name and click the **New File** icon. Name it `hello.py` and press **Enter**.

The `.py` ending tells your computer and VS Code that it's a **Python** file.

items.title: 5. Write your code
items.text:
Click inside the new file and type:
```python
print("Hello World!")
```

items.title: 6. Save it
items.text: Press `Ctrl+S` (`Cmd+S` on a Mac). A **white dot** on the file's tab means there are unsaved changes; it disappears once you save.

blocks.title: Tips for naming files
blocks.text:
- Always end Python files with **.py**
- Use lowercase letters, and underscores instead of spaces: `my_first_program.py`
- Choose names that describe the program
- Don't name files after Python's own tools, such as `random.py` or `math.py`, as this can confuse Python later

blocks.title: Sort these file names
blocks.explanation: Python files need the .py ending, and lowercase names with underscores are easiest to work with.

blocks.title: Two ways to run Python
blocks.text:
## Option 1: the Run button
With `hello.py` open, click the **▷ Run Python File** button in the top-right corner of the editor.

A **terminal** panel opens at the bottom and shows:
```
Hello World!
```
Congratulations, you just ran your first Python program on your own computer! 🎉

## Option 2: the terminal
Open a terminal with **Terminal** → **New Terminal**. Make sure it's in your project folder, then type:
```bash
python hello.py
```
On macOS and Linux, type `python3 hello.py` instead.

> If VS Code asks you to **select an interpreter**, choose the Python 3 version you installed. You can change it any time: press `Ctrl+Shift+P`, type **Python: Select Interpreter** and pick it from the list.

items.title: "python is not recognized"
items.text: Python isn't on your PATH. Run the Python installer again, choose **Modify** or reinstall, and tick **Add python.exe to PATH**. Then restart VS Code. On Windows you can also try `py hello.py`.

items.title: Typing python opens the Microsoft Store
items.text: Windows has a shortcut that points to the Store. Install Python from python.org, or turn off the python.exe **App execution aliases** in Windows Settings.

items.title: There's no Run button
items.text: Check that the Python extension by Microsoft is installed and that your file name ends in **.py**.

items.title: My changes don't show up
items.text: Save the file first (`Ctrl+S`). VS Code runs the saved version.

items.title: "No such file or directory"
items.text: The terminal is in a different folder. Use **File** → **Open Folder…** to open your project folder, then open a new terminal.
